CausalChain: Chronic inflammation in the tumor microenvironment → Activation of cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) → Secretion of IL-6 by CAFs → IL-6 binds to its receptors on tumor and stromal cells → Activation of JAK2 which phosphorylates STAT3 → STAT3 translocates to the nucleus and induces transcription of genes involved in EMT, survival, and epigenetic modifiers (e.g., DNMT1) → Epigenetic reprogramming of CAFs reinforces their immunosuppressive and pro-metastatic phenotype → Sustained secretion of IL-6 and other mediators enhances tumor growth, metastasis, and chemoresistance
Hypothesis: In cancers, IL-6/JAK2/STAT3 signaling not only drives tumor cell proliferation and EMT but also epigenetically reprograms cancer-associated fibroblasts to maintain a pro-tumorigenic and drug-resistant microenvironment. Combining IL-6 pathway inhibition with epigenetic modulators (such as DNMT inhibitors) will disrupt this feed-forward loop, reprogramming CAFs toward an anti-tumor state and thereby enhancing treatment efficacy.
Abstract: The IL-6/JAK2/STAT3 signaling axis is critically implicated in tumor cell proliferation, metastasis, and the formation of an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Emerging evidence indicates that, beyond its tumor cell–autonomous actions, chronic IL-6 production and consequent STAT3 activation may additionally reprogram the surrounding stroma, particularly cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), via epigenetic mechanisms. This reprogramming may perpetuate a self‐reinforcing pro-tumorigenic loop, enhancing cytokine secretion, epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT), and chemoresistance. Here, we hypothesize that combined targeting of IL-6 signaling and its epigenetic downstream effectors in CAFs could re‐educate the tumor microenvironment towards a less supportive state for cancer progression and drug resistance. Testing this strategy may offer a novel therapeutic avenue for overcoming metastasis and improving clinical outcomes.
